en: Points of Controversy Great Fifty-Section First Chapter
The Discourse on Everything Existing: Is it the case that everything exists? Is this logically consistent with the doctrine?
“Yes,” you say.
“Does everything exist everywhere?
One should not speak thus.
Is it the case that everything exists? Yes.
Is it the case that everything exists at all times?
It should not be stated thus.
[If you say] "Everything exists," do you affirm this? Yes.
"Is it the case that everything exists in every way?
"One should not say so.
"Does everything exist?"
“Yes,” you say.
“Is everything present in all things?
One should not speak thus.
Is it the case that "everything exists"? Yes.
Is it the case that "everything exists" by way of non-application? No.
It should not be said so.
Is it the case that "everything exists"?
Yes, it is.
If something does not exist, can it be said that it exists?
One should certainly not say so.
Is everything then existent?
“Yes,” [you say].
“The view that ‘everything exists’—is that view a wrong view, or is that view a right view?
You must not speak thus.
(Condensed. Appropriate Time for Teaching.
Coordination with the Time.
Is the past existent? Yes.
But is it not the case that the past has ceased, has vanished, has changed, has come to an end, and has utterly passed away?
“Yes.
“If the past has ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, and utterly passed away, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘The past exists.’”
Is the future existent? Yes.
But is it not the case that the future is unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, unmanifested, and non-apparent?
“Yes.
“If that which is future is unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, unmanifested, and not made manifest, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘The future exists.’”
Is the present existent, the present unceased, unvanished, unaltered, not come to an end, and not utterly passed away?
Yes.
Is the past existent, the past unceased, unvanished, unaltered, not come to an end, and not utterly passed away?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is it the case that the present exists, the present is born, has become, has come to be, is produced, is fully produced, and has manifested?
Yes, it is.
Is the future existent? Is the future born, become, produced, come-to-be, manifested, and fully manifested?
One should not say so… [as before] … Is the past existent?
Is the past ceased, vanished, changed, gone to its end, and utterly passed away?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is the present existent, yet the present ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, and utterly passed away?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Is the future existent? Is the future unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, unmanifested, and unapparent? Yes.
Is the present existent? Is the present unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, unmanifested, and unapparent?
It should not be said so.
Is past form existent? Yes.
Is it not the case that past form has ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, and utterly passed away?
Yes, it is so.
If past form has ceased... [and so on].
It has passed away; yet, indeed, it should not be said that "past form exists.
Does future form exist?
“Yes.
“Is it not the case that future form is unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, unmanifested, and non-apparent?
“Yes.”
If future form is unborn ...
[and] unmanifested, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
"Future form exists."
"Is present matter existent; is present matter unceased, undispersed, unaltered, not come to an end, and not utterly passed away?
"Yes.
"Is past matter existent; is past matter unceased, undispersed, unaltered, not come to an end, and not utterly passed away?"
It should not be said so.
Is present form existent; is present form born, become, produced, come-to-be, manifested, and made manifest?
Yes.
"Is future form existent? Is future form born, become, produced, come-to-be, manifested, and fully manifested?
One should not say so.
"Is past form existent? Is past form ceased, vanished, changed, passed away, and utterly passed away?"
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is present form existent, yet present form has ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, and utterly passed away?
You should not speak thus.
Is future form existent? Is future form unarisen, non-existent, unborn, unproduced, unmanifested, and unapparent?
Yes.
Is present form existent? Is present form unarisen, non-existent, unborn, unproduced, unmanifested, and unapparent?
It should not be said so.
Is it the case that past feeling exists … pe … that past perception exists, past formations exist, and past consciousness exists?
“Yes.
“But is it not the case that past consciousness has ceased, has vanished, has changed, has come to an end, and has utterly passed away?
“Yes.”
If past consciousness has ceased ...
[and] has passed away, then surely it should not be said:
"Past consciousness exists."
Is future consciousness existent? Yes.
But is it not the case that future consciousness is unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, unmanifested, and non-apparent?
“Yes.
“If future consciousness is unborn … [and so on] … unmanifested,
then indeed, sir, you should not say:”
“Future consciousness exists.
Present consciousness exists; present consciousness is unceased...
[and so on] ...has it not passed away?
“Yes.
“Does past consciousness exist? Is past consciousness unceased?
… [and so on] … has it not come to its end?”
It should not be said so.
Is present consciousness existent? Is present consciousness born?
… [and so on] … is it manifested?
“Yes.
“Then does future consciousness exist? Is future consciousness born?
… [and so on] … is it manifested?”
It should not be said so.
Is past consciousness existent? Is past consciousness ceased?
… [and] has it passed away?
“Yes.
“Does present consciousness exist, yet present consciousness have ceased … [and so on] … have it passed away?”
It should not be said so.
Is future consciousness existent? Is future consciousness unborn? ... [and so on] ...
is it unmanifested?
“Yes.
“Then does present consciousness exist, yet present consciousness be unarisen … [and so on] … unmanifest?”
It should not be said thus.
Is it the case that "the present" or "matter," or "matter" or "the present," are identical, one in meaning, the same, of equal status, and of the same nature, by making the present matter unlovely?
Yes, they are.
Does present matter, when ceasing, abandon its state of being present?
Yes. Does it abandon its nature as matter?
It should not be said so ...

[as before] ... Is "the present" or "matter," or "matter" or "the present"—having made the present matter dear—are these identical, one in meaning, equal, of the same category, and of the same nature?
Yes, they are.
Is present matter, while ceasing, not abandoning its state as matter?
Yes. Does it not abandon its state as present? Yes.
It should not be said thus...
[as before] ...Is "white" or "cloth," or "cloth" or "white," considered identical, one in meaning, the same, equal, and of the same nature by taking the white cloth as the basis?
Yes.
When a white cloth is being dyed, does it abandon its state of being white?
Yes. Does it abandon its state of being cloth? No.
It should not be said thus.
Is "white" or "cloth," or "cloth" or "white," by making the white cloth their object, identical, one in meaning, the same, equal, and of the same nature?
Yes.
Is it not the case that a white cloth, while being dyed, does not abandon its state as cloth?
Yes. Does it not abandon its state as white?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does matter not abandon its state as matter? Yes.
Is form permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
One should not say so.
Is it not the case that because form does not abandon its state as form, form is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?
“Yes.
“If form is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change, then surely it should not be said that ‘form does not abandon its state of being form.’”
“Nibbāna does not abandon its state as Nibbāna; therefore, is Nibbāna permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature?
“Yes.
“Form does not abandon its state as form; therefore, is form permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature?”
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does form not abandon its state of being form, yet is form impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change? Yes.
Does Nibbāna not abandon its state of being Nibbāna; is Nibbāna impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?
One should certainly not say so... [etc.
Does the past exist; does the past not abandon its state of being the past?
“Yes,” you say.
“The future exists; the future does not abandon its future state”?
You should not speak thus.
The past exists; does the past not abandon its state as the past? Yes.
The present exists; does the present not abandon its state as the present?
It should not be said thus...
[as before] ...Is it the case that the future exists, yet the future abandons its future state? Yes.
The past exists; does the past abandon its state of being past?
One should not say so… [and so on] … The present exists;
does the present abandon its state of being present?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does the past exist, and does the past abandon its state of being past?
One should not say so.
The past exists; the past does not abandon its state of being past? Yes.
Is the past permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change? [No.]
It should not be said so...
[as before] ...Is it not the case that the past is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?
Yes, it is.
If the past is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change, then surely it should not be said:
"The past exists; the past does not abandon its state of being past.
[In that case,] would you say that because Nibbāna exists and Nibbāna does not abandon its state of being Nibbāna, therefore Nibbāna is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
“Yes,” [you say].
“The past exists; the past does not abandon its state of being past; therefore, the past is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
You should not speak thus… [and so on].
"The past exists; the past does not abandon its state of being past; the past is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change"?—Yes.
"Nirvana exists; Nirvana does not abandon its state of being Nirvana; Nirvana is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change"?—[No].
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is past form existent? Is past form not abandoning its state as past?
Yes.
"Does future form exist? Does future form not abandon its state of being future?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ... "Does past form exist? Does past form not abandon its state of being past? One should not say so.
“Yes,” you say.
“Does present matter exist, and does present matter not abandon its state of being present?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] … No.
Future matter exists; does future matter abandon its state of being future? Yes.
Past matter exists; does past matter abandon its state of being past?
It should not be said thus ... [as before] ...
Present matter exists; does present matter abandon its state of being present? Yes.
Past matter exists; does past matter abandon its state of being past?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...Past matter exists; does past matter not abandon its state of being past?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is past form permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
“One should certainly not say so. …pe…
Is it not the case that past form is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?
Yes, it is.
If past form is impermanent … [and so on] … [then it follows].
[It is] subject to change; yet surely it should not be said:
“Past form exists, and past form does not abandon its state of being past.
Is it the case that Nibbāna exists, that Nibbāna does not abandon its state of being Nibbāna, and that Nibbāna is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does past form exist? Does past form not abandon its state of being past? Is past form permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
You should not say so… [and so on]…
"Past form exists; past form does not abandon its state of being past; past form is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change"?—Yes.
"Nirvana exists; nirvana does not abandon its state of being nirvana; nirvana is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change"?—No.
It should not be said thus … [as above] … past feeling exists … past perception exists …
"Past formations exist...
past consciousness exists; does past consciousness not abandon its state of being past?
"Yes."
"Does future consciousness exist? Does future consciousness not abandon its future state?
One should not say this... [and so on] ...
"Does past consciousness exist? Does past consciousness not abandon its past state? One should not say this.
“Yes.
“Present consciousness exists; present consciousness does not abandon its state of being present?
“One should not say that … [and so on].”
Future consciousness exists; does future consciousness abandon its state of being future? Yes.
Past consciousness exists; does past consciousness abandon its state of being past?
It should not be said thus ... [as before] ...
Is present consciousness existent, yet does present consciousness abandon its state of being present?
Yes.
"Does past consciousness exist? Does past consciousness abandon its state of being past?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
"Does past consciousness exist? Does past consciousness not abandon its state of being past? One should not say so.
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is past consciousness permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
"Is it not the case that past consciousness is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?
"Yes.
"If past consciousness is indeed impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change, then surely you should not say—"
“Past consciousness exists; past consciousness does not abandon its state of being past.
Is it the case that Nibbāna exists, Nibbāna does not abandon its state of being Nibbāna, and Nibbāna is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
Yes, it is.
“Does past consciousness exist? Does past consciousness not abandon its state of being past? Is past consciousness permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?
“One should not say so…” “…Is past consciousness impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?”
“Yes.
“Nibbāna exists; Nibbāna does not abandon its state of being Nibbāna; yet Nibbāna is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change?
“One should certainly not say so…” [and so forth].
1. Purification of Statements:
"Does the past exist?
Yes, it does.
If the past exists, then it is wrong to say "the past exists.
Or if the past exists, then it is wrong to say "there is a past.
Does the future exist?
“Yes.
“If it is so that the future exists, then it is wrong to say ‘the future exists.
Or if it is so that the future does exist, then it is wrong to say ‘there is a future.’”
Having been future, it becomes present?
Yes. Is that very same thing which was future now present? No.
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is that which is future the same as that which is present? Yes.
"Having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes"?
One should not say so... [as before] ...
"Having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes"?
“Yes,” you say.
“Having not been, one does not exist; having not been, one does not exist”?
You should not speak thus… [as before]… No, indeed.
Having been present, does it become past?
Yes. Is that very same present thing the past? No.
It should not be said thus ...
[as before] ... Is that which is present the same as that which is past? Yes.
"Having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes"?
One should not say so... [as before] ...
"Having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes"?
“Yes,” [you say].
But should it not be said that “having not been, one does not exist; having not been, one does not exist”?
You must certainly not say so … [and so on] …
“Having been future, it becomes present; having been present, it becomes past”?—Yes.
“Is that very same thing which was future now present, and now past”?—No.
It should not be said thus ...
[as before] ... Is that which is future the same as that which is present, and that which is present the same as that which is past? Yes.
"Having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes"?
One should not say so... [as before] ...
"Having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes"?
“Yes,” you say.
“Having not been, one does not exist; having not been, one does not exist”?
You should not speak thus.
2. Discussion on Past Eye, Visible Objects, and so forth.
Is it the case that the past eye exists, visible objects exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, and attention exists?
Yes, it is.
Does one see a past form with a past eye?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...Is there a past ear, are there sounds, is there ear-consciousness, is there space, and is there attention? Yes.
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does one hear a past sound with a past ear?
One should not say so … [and so on] …
Is it the case that there is past nose, there are odors, there is nose-consciousness, there is air, and there is attention? Yes.
Does one smell a past odor with a past nose?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … “The past tongue exists,
tastes exist, tongue-consciousness exists, water exists, and attention exists”? Yes.
Does one taste a past taste with a past tongue?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Does a past body exist, do past tangibles exist, does past body-consciousness exist, does earth exist, and does attention exist?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does one touch a past tangible object with a past body?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Is it the case that the past mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists?
Yes. Does one cognize a past mental object by means of a past mind?
It should not be said so… [as before]… Is it the case that the future eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, and attention exists?
Yes, it is.
Does one see a future form with a future eye?
One should not say so … [and so on] … Does a future ear exist?
There is the nose … there is the tongue … there is the body …
Is it the case that there is mind, there are mental objects, there is mind-consciousness, there is the physical basis, and there is attention? Yes.
Does one cognize a future mental object with a future mind?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Present eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, attention exists; does one see a present visible form with a present eye?
Yes.
The past eye exists; visible forms exist; eye-consciousness exists; light exists; attention exists. [If so,] does one see a past visible form with a past eye?
One should not say so… [and so on]… The present ear exists… [and so on]…
The nose exists … the tongue exists … the body exists …
The mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; [therefore] one cognizes a present mental object by means of a present mind?
Yes.
The past mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; [therefore] one cognizes a past mental object by means of a past mind?
It should not be said so … [as before] … Present eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, attention exists; does one see a present visible form with a present eye?
Yes.
The future eye exists; visible forms exist; eye-consciousness exists; light exists; attention exists. [If so,] does one see a future visible form with a future eye?
One should not say this...
[and so on] ...the present ear exists... [and so on].
The nose exists … the tongue exists … the body exists …
"The mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; does one cognize a present mental object by means of a present mind?"—Yes.

"Does the future mind exist, do mental objects exist, does mind-consciousness exist, does the physical basis exist, and does attention exist; does one cognize a future mental object by means of a future mind?"—[Yes.]

It should not be said so … [as before] … The past eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, and attention exists; yet one does not see a past visible form with a past eye?
Yes, that is so.
Is it not the case that the present eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, and attention exists, yet one does not see a present visible form with a present eye?
One should not say so … [and so on] … the past ear exists … [and so on].
The nose exists … the tongue exists … the body exists …
The mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; yet it is not by means of a past mind that one cognizes a past mental object?
Yes.

Present mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; yet it is not by means of a present mind that one cognizes a present mental object?

It should not be said so … [as before] … Future eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, and attention exists; yet one does not see a future visible form with a future eye?
Yes.
The present eye exists, visible forms exist, eye-consciousness exists, light exists, and attention exists; yet one does not see a present visible form with a present eye?
You should not say this...
[and so on] ...the future ear exists... [and so on].
The nose exists … the tongue exists … the body exists …
The mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; yet, one does not cognize a future mental object by means of a future mind?
Yes.

The present mind exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, the physical basis exists, and attention exists; yet, one does not cognize a present mental object by means of a present mind? No.
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … 3.
Discussion on Knowledge of the Past, etc.
Is there knowledge of the past?
“Yes.
“Does one perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Does one perform what is to be done by means of that knowledge? Yes.
Does one fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path by means of that knowledge?
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is there knowledge of the future? Yes.
Does one perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Does one perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does one, by means of that knowledge, fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path?
You should not say so… [and so on]… No.
Is there knowledge of the present? Yes. Does one perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge?
Yes. Is there knowledge of the past? Yes. Does one perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge? Yes.
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is there present knowledge?
By means of that knowledge, one fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realizes cessation, and develops the path?
Yes.
Is there knowledge of the past? By means of that knowledge, does one fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Is there present knowledge? By means of that knowledge, does one perform what is to be done by knowledge?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Does future knowledge exist, and does one perform the function of knowing by means of that knowledge?
[The respondent replies: “One should certainly not say so. …pe…
Is there knowledge of the present? By means of that knowledge, one fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realizes its cessation, and develops the path?
Yes.
Is there knowledge of the future? By means of that knowledge, one fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realizes its cessation, and develops the path?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is there past knowledge,
and yet one does not perform the function of knowledge with that knowledge? Yes.
Is there knowledge of the present, yet one does not perform the function of knowledge with that knowledge?

One should certainly not say so … [and so on] … Is there past knowledge, yet one does not fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path with that knowledge? One should certainly not say so.
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is there present knowledge, yet by that knowledge one does not fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path?
One should certainly not say so … [and so on] …
Is there knowledge of the future, and yet one does not perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge?
Yes. Is there knowledge of the present, and yet one does not perform the function of knowledge by means of that knowledge? Yes.

It should not be said so … [as before] … Is there knowledge of the future, yet by that knowledge one does not fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, or develop the path? Yes.
Is there knowledge of the present, yet by that knowledge one does not fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path?
One should certainly not say so… [as before]… 4.
Discussion on the Arhat and Others.
Is there past lust in an Arahant? Yes.
Is the Arahant possessed of lust because of that lust?
It should not be said so ... [as before] ...
Is it the case that a past hatred exists for an Arahant? Yes.
Is an Arahant possessed of hatred because of that past hatred?
One should not say so …pe… Does an Arahant possess past delusion?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is an arahant deluded by that delusion?
You must not say so …pe…
Is it the case that a past conceit exists for an arahant?
Yes. Is the arahant identical to that conceit?
It should not be said so ... [as before] ...
Is it the case that a past view exists for an Arahant? Yes.
Is an Arahant one who possesses that view?
One should not say so …pe… Does past doubt exist for an Arahant?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is an Arahant possessed of doubt because of that doubt?
You must not say so … [and so on] …
Is there past sloth in an Arahant? Yes.
Is the Arahant, because of that sloth, a deceiver?
It should not be said thus ... [as before] ...
Is it the case that past restlessness exists for an Arahant? Yes.
Is an Arahant possessed of restlessness because of that restlessness?
One should not say so …pe… Does past lack of moral shame exist for an Arahant?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is an Arahant, because of that lack of moral shame (ahirika), one who possesses moral shame (saahirika)?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Is there past lack of moral dread in an Arahant? Yes.
Is the Arahant, by virtue of that lack of moral dread, one who possesses lack of moral dread?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is it the case that a non-returner possesses past personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)? Yes.
Is the non-returner one who possesses that view?
One should not say so …pe… the non-returner has past doubt.
Is there past adherence to rules and observances?
Is there past lust for sensual pleasures that remains as a subtle residue?
Is there past ill will that remains as a subtle residue?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is a non-returner one whose mind is corrupted by that ill will?
You should not say so… [and so on].
Is past personality-belief present in a once-returner? Yes.
Is the once-returner possessed of that view because of that view?
It should not be said thus...
[and so on] ... for a once-returner, past doubt exists;
past adherence to rites and rituals exists.
Is there past gross sensual desire?
… Is there past gross ill will? Yes.
Is a once-returner one whose mind is corrupted by that corruption?
One should not say so… [and so on] … Does a stream-enterer possess past personality-belief?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is a stream-enterer one who possesses that view?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
For one who has entered the stream, there exists past doubt;
there exists past adherence to rules and observances;
there exists past lust leading to states of deprivation.
Is there past hatred that leads to a state of deprivation?
Yes. Is there past delusion that leads to a state of deprivation? Yes.
Is a stream-enterer deluded by that delusion?
One should not say so... [and so on].
Does an ordinary person possess past lust? Is an ordinary person possessed of lust because of that lust?
“Yes,” you say.
“Does a past lust exist in an Arahant? Is an Arahant ‘one possessed of lust’ because of that lust?
You must not say so … [and so on] …
Does a worldling possess past hatred …pe… does a worldling possess past lack of moral dread?
[If you say] "Yes," [then we ask: Is that worldling, by virtue of that past lack of moral dread, a person of no moral dread?
[If you say] "Yes."
The Arahant possesses past lack of moral dread; is the Arahant, because of that lack of moral dread, one who lacks moral dread?
One should not say so… [as before] … The worldling possesses past personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); is the worldling, because of that belief, one who holds such a belief?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does the non-returner possess past personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), and is the non-returner one who possesses that view?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Does a worldling have past doubt? ... [and so on] ...
Does a worldling have past latent ill will? Is the worldling one whose mind is corrupted by that ill will? Yes.
Does a non-returner possess past ill-will that is still lingering? Is a non-returner one whose mind is corrupted by that ill-will?
One should not say so… [and so forth]… Does an ordinary person possess past personality-belief? Is an ordinary person one who holds such a view because of that belief?
“Yes,” you say.
“Does a once-returner possess past personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), and is that once-returner ‘one who possesses view’ by virtue of that view?
You must not say so … [and so on].
Does a worldling have past doubt? ...
Does a worldling have past gross ill-will, such that the worldling is one whose mind is corrupted by that ill-will? Yes.
Does a once-returner possess past gross ill-will, such that the once-returner is one whose mind is corrupted by that ill-will?
One should not say so... [and so forth].
Does an ordinary person possess past personality-belief, such that the ordinary person is one who holds that view?
“Yes,” you say.
“Does past personality-belief exist for one who has entered the stream, and is that stream-enterer possessed of views because of that view?
You must not say so … [and so on] …
Does a worldling have past doubt? ... [and so on] ...
Does a worldling have past delusion leading to states of deprivation? Is the worldling deluded by that delusion? Yes.
Does the stream-enterer possess past delusion leading to the states of deprivation, and is the stream-enterer deluded by that delusion?
One should not say so … [and so on] … Does the Arhat possess past lust, and yet is the Arhat possessed of lust by that lust?
“Yes.
“Then, does a worldling possess past lust, yet is not a worldling ‘one with lust’ because of that lust?
“One should certainly not say so. … [as before] …
Does the Arahant have past hatred …pe… does he have past lack of moral dread?
And yet, is the Arahant not a person of lack of moral dread because of that past lack of moral dread?
Yes, he is.
An ordinary person possesses past lack of moral dread; yet would you say that the ordinary person is "one characterized by lack of moral dread" because of that past lack of moral dread?
Certainly not... [as before] ...An Anāgāmin possesses past personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); yet would you say that the Anāgāmin is "one possessed of personality-belief" because of that belief?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does a worldling possess past views of self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), yet is that worldling not ‘one who holds such views’ because of those views?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Does a non-returner possess past doubt …pe… does he possess past latent ill will,
yet is the non-returner not one whose mind is corrupted by that ill will? Yes.
Does a worldling possess past malice that persists as a subtle residue, yet the worldling is not said to have a mind corrupted by that malice?
One should not say so… [and so on]… Does a once-returner possess past personality-belief, yet the once-returner is not said to be possessed of views because of that view?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does a worldling possess past views of self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), yet is that worldling not ‘one who holds views’ (*sadiṭṭhika*) because of those views?
You must not say so … [and so on] …
Does a once-returner possess past doubt …pe… does he possess past gross ill will, yet is the once-returner not one whose mind is corrupted by that ill will?
Yes.
The worldling has past gross ill-will; yet, would you say that the worldling is one whose mind is corrupted by that ill-will?

One should not say so… [and so on]… The stream-enterer has past personality-belief; yet, would you say that the stream-enterer is one who holds such views because of that belief? One should not say so.
“Yes,” you say.
“Does a worldling possess past views of self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), yet is that worldling not ‘one who holds such views’ (*sadiṭṭhika*) because of those views?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Does a stream-enterer possess past doubt …pe… does he possess past delusion leading to states of deprivation, yet is the stream-enterer not deluded by that delusion?
Yes, he is.
Does a worldling possess past delusion that leads to rebirth in the states of misery, yet the worldling is not possessed by that delusion?
One should not say so… [as before]… 5.
Discussion on Past Hands, etc.
Is it the case that past hands exist? Yes.
If past hands exist, is the act of taking up and laying down discernible in them?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Do past feet exist? Yes.
Is it when there are past steps that advancing and retreating are discerned?
You should not say so...
[and so on] ...Do past fingers exist?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is contraction and extension perceived when past bodies exist?
You should not say so …pe…
Is it the case that there is a past womb? Yes.
If there is a past womb, are hunger and thirst manifested?
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … Is the past body existent? Yes.
Is the past body subject to exertion and restraint, subject to cutting and breaking, and common to crows, vultures, and hawks?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...would poison enter the past body, would a weapon enter it, or would fire enter it?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … it is possible to bind a past body with a wooden shackle, to bind it with a rope shackle, to bind it with an iron chain shackle,
to bind it with a village shackle, to bind it with a town shackle, or to bind it with a city shackle.
To bind him, to bind him with the bonds of the countryside, to bind him with the fivefold bonds including the neck?
One should not say so… [etc.
… Does past water exist?
“Yes,” you say.
“Does that water perform the function of water?
You must not say so … [and so on] …
Is there past fire? Yes.
Does it perform the function of fire by means of that fire?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is past air existent? Yes.
“Does one perform what is to be done by means of that wind?
One should not say so… [as before]… 6.
Discussion on the Conjunction of Past Aggregates, etc.
Is the past aggregate of form existent? Is the future aggregate of form existent? Is the present aggregate of form existent?
Yes. Are these three aggregates of form?
It should not be said thus...
[as before] ...Is it the case that the five past aggregates exist, the five future aggregates exist, and the five present aggregates exist?
Yes, they do.
"Are there fifteen aggregates?
"One should not say so... [and so on].
"Does the past eye-base exist? Does the future eye-base exist? Does the present eye-base exist?"
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are there three eye-bases?
One should not say so …pe…
Are there twelve bases that are past? Are there twelve bases that are future? Are there twelve bases that are present? Yes.
Are they, then, thirty-six bases?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is it the case that the past eye-element exists, the future eye-element exists, and the present eye-element exists?
Yes.
Are there three eye-elements?
One should not say so …pe… Are there eighteen elements that are past,
eighteen elements that are future, and eighteen elements that are present?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are there fifty-four elements?
One should not speak thus …pe… [end of section].
Is there a past eye-faculty? Is there a future eye-faculty? Is there a present eye-faculty? Yes.
Are these three eye-faculties?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … “The twenty-two faculties of the past exist; the twenty-two faculties of the future exist; the twenty-two faculties of the present exist”?
Yes, they do.
"Are there sixty-six faculties?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...Is it the case that there was a past universal monarch, there is a future universal monarch, and there is a present universal monarch?
“Yes.
[If you say this,] would it be right to say that the simultaneous presence of three kings who are universal monarchs occurs?
Certainly not; [it should not be said so] …pe… .
Is there a Perfectly Enlightened One of the past? Is there a Perfectly Enlightened One of the future? Is there a Perfectly Enlightened One of the present? Yes.
Does the simultaneous presence of three Perfectly Enlightened Ones occur?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … 7.
Discussion on the Purification of Terms:
Does the past exist?
“Yes,” he said.
“Does ‘the past’ exist?
“It may exist as the past, and it may not exist as the past.”
Understand this refutation:
If the past exists, then the past might exist; it might be that the past is not the past, and therefore the past is not the past, and the not-past is the past.
As for what you said there—
“If it must be said: ‘The past exists; there may be the past; there may be what is not yet past; therefore the past is what is not yet past, and what is not yet past is the past’—that is false.
But if the past is not what is not yet past, and what is not yet past is not the past, then indeed, sir, you should not say:”
“Does the past exist? Does it exist? Might the past exist? Or might there not be a past?
Regarding this, you say:
“It must indeed be said:”
‘The past exists; it may exist as the past, it may indeed be the past; therefore the past is indeed the past, and what is indeed the past is the past’—this is wrong.
Is it the case that the future exists?
Yes, it does.
"Is there the future?
"There may be the future; there may be no future.
Understand this as a refutation.

If the future exists, it would follow that the future both exists and does not exist; and because it both exists and does not exist, the future would be non-future, and the non-future would be the future.
As for what you said there—"It should indeed be stated..."—it is thus.
“It is wrong to say: ‘The future exists; there may be a future; there may indeed be a future; by that [reason] the future is indeed a future;
indeed a future is the future. If indeed the future is not ‘indeed a future’ nor ‘indeed a future is the future,’ then surely it should not be said:
‘The future exists; there may be a future; there may indeed be a future.’”
As for what you said there—"It should indeed be stated:
'The future exists; the future may exist; the future may not exist; by that [reason] the future is the future; the future is the future'"—that is incorrect.
Is it the case that the present exists? Yes.
Does the present exist?
"There may be a present, and there may not be a present.
Understand this as a refutation.

If it is the case that "the present exists" and "there may be a present, and there may not be a present," then by that [very fact], it follows that the present is not the present, and what is not the present is the present.
As for what you said there—"It should indeed be stated:
'The present exists; the present may exist, it may not exist; by that [reasoning], the present is not the present, and what is not the present is the present'"—that is wrong.
But if it is neither "the present is not the present" nor "the present is the present," then indeed you should not say:
"The present exists; there may be the present, there may be no present.
As for what you have said therein—
“It must be said:
‘The present exists; there may be the present, there may be that which is not the present; therefore, the present is not the present, and that which is not the present is the present’”—this is false.
Is nibbāna existent?
“Yes,” he said.
“Is there Nibbāna? “There is;
it may be Nibbāna, and it may not be Nibbāna.”
Understand this refutation:

If indeed there is Nibbāna, then it might be that Nibbāna exists, or it might be that Nibbāna does not exist; therefore, what you say therein—that "Nibbāna is not Nibbāna" and "what is not Nibbāna is Nibbāna"—is incorrect.
“If it must be said:
‘Nibbāna exists; there may be Nibbāna, there may be no Nibbāna; therefore, Nibbāna is not Nibbāna, and what is not Nibbāna is Nibbāna,’ that is false.
But if Nibbāna is neither ‘not Nibbāna’ nor ‘what is not Nibbāna is Nibbāna,’ then indeed, you should not say:”
“Nibbāna exists; there may be Nibbāna, or there may not be Nibbāna.
Regarding what you said therein:
indeed, it must be stated—
‘Nibbāna exists; there might be Nibbāna, there might not be Nibbāna; by that [reasoning] Nibbāna is not Nibbāna, what is not Nibbāna is Nibbāna’—this is wrong.
8. Proof by Sutta:
It should not be said—
“Does the past exist? Does the future exist?
— “Yes.
But was it not said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior;
far or near—all that is called the aggregate of form.
Whatever feeling there is...”
Whatever kind of perception...
whatever kind of volitional formations...
whatever kind of consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—
“This is called the aggregate of consciousness.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
"Therefore, indeed, the past exists; the future exists.
"The past exists; the future exists?
"Yes."
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, there are these three ways of linguistic expression, ways of designation, ways of description that are unmixed, have never been mixed, are not being mixed, will not be mixed, and are not rejected by wise recluses and brahmins.
Which three?”
“Bhikkhus, whatever form is past, ceased, vanished, and changed is reckoned as ‘it was,’ designated as ‘it was,’ and described as ‘it was’;
it is not reckoned as ‘it is,’ nor is it reckoned as ‘it will be. Whatever feeling... [and so on for the other aggregates]...”
Whatever perception...
whatever formations...
whatever consciousness has passed away, ceased, vanished, and changed—that is reckoned as ‘it was,’ that is designated as ‘it was,’ that is described as ‘it was.’
For that, there is no designation as "it exists," nor is there for it a designation as "it will exist.
Monks, whatever form is unborn and unmanifested, the term "it will exist" is its designation, "it will exist" is its conventional expression, "it will exist" is its description;
for it there is no designation as "it exists," nor is there for it a designation as "it has been."
Whatever feeling...
whatever perception...
whatever volitional formations...
That consciousness which is unborn and unmanifested, for which there is the designation “it will be,” the appellation “it will be,” and the description “it will be”—
for that there is no designation “it exists” and no designation “it was.
But that form, monks, which is born and manifested, for which there is the designation “it exists,” the appellation “it exists,” and the description “it exists”;

For him there is no conceptualization that "it was," nor is there for him the conceptualization that "it will be. This applies to whatever feeling there is … and whatever perception there is … [and so forth].
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness has been born and manifested, for that there is the designation "it exists," for that there is the convention "it exists," for that there is the description "it exists";
for it there is no designation "it was," nor is there for it the designation "it will be."

“Monks, these three ways of linguistic expression, ways of designation, and ways of description are unadulterated, have never been adulterated, are not being adulterated, and will not be adulterated; they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.

Even those, monks, who were the Ukkalā Vassabhajjhas—proponents of non-causality, proponents of non-action, and proponents of nihilism—even they did not consider these three ways of linguistic expression, ways of designation, and ways of description to be censurable or to be rejected.”
For what reason?
“Out of fear of blame, censure, and reproach.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes,” [he replies].
“In that case, it should not be said:
‘The past exists; the future exists.’”
"Does the past exist?
"Yes.
"Did not the Venerable Phagguna say this to the Blessed One?"

“Is there, venerable sir, such an eye by which one, when designating, could designate those Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferation of conceptualization has been cut off, the course of rebirth has been severed, the round has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering?
Is there, venerable sir, such a tongue...

[and so on] ...is there, venerable sir, such a mind by which one, when designating, could designate those Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferation of conceptualization has been cut off, the course of rebirth has been severed, the round has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering?”

“Phagguna, there is no such eye by which one could describe, as having passed away in the past, those Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferation of conceptualization has been cut off, the cycle of rebirth has been severed, the round has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering.
Phagguna, there is no such tongue...

[and so on] ...Phagguna, is there not such a mind by which one could describe, as having passed away in the past, those Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferation of conceptualization has been cut off, the cycle of rebirth has been severed, the round has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering?”
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“The past exists.
Does the past exist? Yes.
Did not the Venerable Nandaka say this:
“In the past there was greed, which on that day was unwholesome; that is no longer present now, and thus this is wholesome.
In the past there was hatred...”
"Formerly there was delusion; that was unwholesome. That does not exist now; this is wholesome.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said that "the past exists.
It should not be said—
“Does the future exist?”—
“Yes.
But was it not said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, if there is lust for physical food, if there is delight, if there is craving,
consciousness becomes established there and comes to growth.
Wherever consciousness becomes established and comes to growth, there is the descent of name-and-form.”
Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations.
Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is future birth, aging, and death.
“Wherever there is future birth, aging, and death, monks, I say that it is accompanied by sorrow, with dust, and with despair.
This is true, monks, regarding the nutriment of contact… and regarding the nutriment of mental volition.”
“Bhikkhus, if there is lust for the nutriment consciousness, if there is delight...
[as before] ...I say that it is with dust and with fever.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes,” [you say].
“In that case, the future exists.
Does the future exist?
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, if there is no lust for physical nutriment, no delight, and no craving;’”
There, consciousness is unestablished and does not come to growth.
Where consciousness is unestablished and does not come to growth, there is no descent of name-and-form.
Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations.
Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of renewed existence in the future.
Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no birth, aging, and death in the future.
Where there is no birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is sorrowless, dustless, and free from despair.
If, monks, there is no lust, no delight... [as before] ...in the nutriment contact, in the nutriment mental volition,
or in the nutriment consciousness, [then one is liberated].
“I say that it is without king and without affliction.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said that "the future exists.
The Discussion on the Existence of All Things is concluded.
